==Problem==
A poll asked a number of people if they liked solving mathematics problems. Exactly <imath>74\%</imath> answered "yes." What is the fewest possible number of people who could have been asked the question?

<imath>\textbf{(A)}\ 10 \qquad \textbf{(B)}\ 20 \qquad \textbf{(C)}\ 25 \qquad \textbf{(D)}\ 50 \qquad \textbf{(E)}\ 100</imath>

==Solution 1==


Well, we use our critical thinking skills to know that you can’t have .<imath>5</imath> or .<imath>7</imath> people (or any fraction for that matter). So, we will be like me while taking this test and do each answer individually (starting from smallest) until one gives us a whole number. 
which in this case that is <imath>\boxed{ \textbf{(D) } 50}</imath>. (although this is quite slow so I’d use the other methods posted)
~pereena come on let's think positively, ok?

==Solution 2==

Let <imath>n</imath> be the number of people. Then, <imath>\frac{74}{100} n</imath> like to do math (I think I am one of them). <imath>\frac{74}{100}</imath> simplifies down to <imath>\frac{37}{50}</imath>, so the remaining people who don't like math (haters just hate I guess) would also fall under the <imath>50</imath> denominator category. The answer is <imath>\boxed{50}</imath>

~Pinotation

==Solution 3==
We start by trying every answer from smallest to greatest. We have that <imath>10</imath> is the smallest choice, so we try this. If we polled <imath>10</imath> people, then <imath>7.6</imath> must have said yes, which is clearly impossible, since fractional people can't exist so we discard this answer. If we continue in this matter, we can find that the answer is <imath>\boxed{ \textbf{(D) }50}</imath>. 

~Baihly2024

==Solution 4==
If <imath>10</imath> people are polled, then <imath>74</imath> must be divisible by <imath>10</imath>, but it's not, so it is not <imath>10</imath> people. If 20 people are polled, then <imath>74</imath> must be divisible by <imath>5</imath>, but it's not, so it is not <imath>20</imath> people. If <imath>25</imath> people are polled, then <imath>74</imath> must be divisible by <imath>4</imath>, but it's not, so it is not <imath>25</imath> people. If <imath>50</imath> people are polled, then <imath>76</imath> must be divisible by <imath>2</imath>, which it is, so our answer is <imath>\boxed{ \textbf{(D) }50}</imath>. 

~Yuhao2012

==Solution 5==

Our percent is 74
Assuming the people are in whole numbers…

If it is A) 10, then the percent will have to be a multiple of <imath> \frac{100}{10} </imath> = 10

If it is B) 20, then the percent will have to be a multiple of <imath> \frac {100}{20} </imath> = 5

If it is C) 25, then the percent will have to be a multiple of <imath> \frac {100}{25} </imath> = 4

It it is D) 50, then the percent will have to be a multiple of <imath> \frac {100}{50} </imath> = 2

If it is E) 100, then the percent will have to be a multiple of <imath> \frac {100}{100} </imath> = 1

In this case, 74 only fits D and E, and because D is less, <imath>\boxed{ \textbf{(D) }50}</imath> is the correct answer.

==Solution 6==

We can see that <imath>74 \% = \frac{74}{100}</imath> by definition. This fraction can be simplified to <imath>\frac{37}{50}</imath>, meaning <imath>37</imath> out of <imath>50</imath> people said "Yes". Since <imath>\gcd(37,50) = 1</imath>, if this fraction was divided any further, we would have fractional numerator and denominator, which is clearly impossible. Therefore, the minimum number of people surveyed was <imath>\boxed{ \textbf{(D) } 50}</imath>.
~Ingeniouspeacock36
